messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 43
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 77

She is forty-three, a physical therapist from Oceania, and when she tells the story now, she still begins with the sound. Not the sight of it, not even the moment she understands what has happened, but the sudden crack of impact in the clinic gym, followed by a man’s cry that seems to split the room in two.

It happens late on a Friday, at the end of a long week. She is working with an older patient recovering from a spinal surgery, a careful man she has seen for months. They are practicing transfers and standing balance, something they have done many times before. She remembers feeling tired but confident, moving on habit and training. As he shifts his weight, she reaches to correct his position. Later she replays this detail endlessly—whether her hand is too quick, whether she asks him to turn too soon, whether she misses the first sign that he is losing balance. He falls hard. In the scramble to catch him, both of them go down awkwardly. There is a sickening twist, then shouting for help.

The injury is serious. She rides with him in the ambulance because she cannot bear not knowing. At the hospital she stands in her scrubs, hands trembling, listening as the emergency physician explains fractures, surgical complications, and the possibility of a long recovery. She apologizes to the patient, then to his wife, then to anyone who will listen. No one yells at her. The patient’s wife is pale and stunned, and that is somehow worse. Over the next few days, she gives statements, fills out incident reports, answers questions from supervisors. She goes home but does not feel she has left the hospital. The scene follows her into the shower, into bed, into the moments just before sleep when she sees his body falling again and jerks awake with her heart pounding.

At first she tells herself the horror will fade. She has worked in rehabilitation long enough to know that bad outcomes happen, even to careful clinicians. But this feels different because her own body is inside the memory. She cannot stop checking the sequence for the exact second she failed him. She wakes at 3 a.m. hearing the impact and lies rigid beside her partner, afraid to move. If she does sleep, she dreams of trying to hold up patient after patient while her hands slide away uselessly. In the morning she feels sick before work. In the clinic gym, the parallel bars, gait belts, transfer boards—ordinary tools she has used for years—suddenly look dangerous.

She becomes watchful in a way that exhausts her. During sessions, she positions chairs behind everyone, calls coworkers over “just in case,” and keeps one hand hovering near each patient even during simple tasks. Her notes take twice as long because she rereads them, terrified she has missed something. If a patient stumbles, even slightly, her whole body floods with heat. She hears herself speaking too brightly, too fast. Some colleagues interpret her caution as professionalism. Others begin gently teasing her for being “extra careful.” She laughs with them and then goes to the staff bathroom and cries silently with a paper towel pressed over her mouth.

Outside work, her world narrows. She stops driving the route past the hospital where the patient was admitted. She avoids the section of the clinic where the fall happened and trades shifts to stay away from that gym. At home, her partner notices she is no longer cooking, no longer making weekend plans, no longer answering messages from friends. When asked what is wrong, she says she is tired. It is easier than saying that she no longer trusts her own judgment, that every decision feels potentially catastrophic. Her partner reaches for her at night and she startles so sharply that both of them go still. Afterwards she apologizes, ashamed, but also irritated by being touched when she is trying so hard to keep herself together.

What disturbs her most is not only fear but the moral weight of it. She chose a profession built around helping bodies heal, and now she experiences her own hands as dangerous. Sometimes in session she looks at a patient waiting for instruction and has a brief, dizzy feeling that she should not be allowed near anyone. She begins to dread work on Sunday mornings, then on Saturday night, then by Friday afternoon. Yet staying home is not a relief either. In the quiet, her mind returns to the patient and his wife. She searches online for updates she cannot ethically seek, imagines the cost of surgery, the months of pain, the altered future radiating outward from one moment in her care.

Months later, she still lives as if the accident is about to happen again. She scans rooms for hazards, flinches at sudden noises, and feels a jolt of panic whenever someone loses balance near her, even in public. Her partner says she seems far away, and she knows it is true. Part of her remains in that clinic gym, hearing the crack of impact, trying over and over to reach back one second earlier.
